property_summary: For every 4-byte interfaceId input, the reference contract returns true for IERC165's interface id (0x01ffc9a7) and for IAccessControl's id when queried; the mutant returns false for IERC165 (since it only recognizes IAccessControl), so there exists some interfaceId (e.g., IERC165 id) that the mutant reports differently while the reference always reports IERC165 support true.

For every 4-byte interface id, the correct contract C returns true for IERC165's interface id (0x01ffc9a7) when queried via supportsInterface, while the mutant that only checks IAccessControl will return false for IERC165's id — so the rule: supportsInterface(type(IERC165).interfaceId) always returns true; the mutant breaks this for some input (the IERC165 id).

For every 4-byte interfaceId, the reference contract's supportsInterface returns true when queried with the IERC165 interface id (type(IERC165).interfaceId) while the mutant that only checks IAccessControl will return false for the IERC165 id — so the property is that supportsInterface(type(IERC165).interfaceId) must be true for the correct contract and will be false for the mutant for that input.

For every input ifaceId, the reference C reports true when asked supportsInterface(type(IERC165).interfaceId) (it always supports IERC165), while the mutant that only recognizes IAccessControl will return false for the IERC165 id — so the property: calling supportsInterface with the IERC165 interface id must succeed (not revert) and return true for the correct contract.

For every 4-byte interface id, the reference contract's supportsInterface returns true for the ERC165 interface id (type(IERC165).interfaceId) while the mutant that only checks IAccessControl will return false for that id, so the universal rule is: calling supportsInterface with type(IERC165).interfaceId completes and returns true; the mutant violates this for that interface id.

For every interfaceId, the reference contract's supportsInterface returns true for IERC165's interfaceId (0x01ffc9a7) while the mutant that always returns false will report false for that interfaceId, so the rule is that supportsInterface(type(IERC165).interfaceId) must be true; the mutant breaks this for that interfaceId.

For every bytes4 id, the reference contract returns true for supportsInterface(type(IERC165).interfaceId) (i.e. it reports support for IERC165) while the mutant that always returns false will return false for that well-known IERC165 interface id.

For every interfaceId equal to type(ERC165).interfaceId (i.e. ERC165's own selector), the correct contract C.supportsInterface(interfaceId) returns true (reports support) while the mutant that always returns false will report false for that same interfaceId; the test fuzzes a bytes4 and asserts that if the fuzzed bytes4 equals type(IERC165).interfaceId then supportsInterface must return true (reference) which the mutant will violate for that input.

For every bytes4 interfaceId equal to type(IAccessControl).interfaceId, C.supportsInterface(interfaceId) must return true (the reference advertises IAccessControl support); the mutant that always returns false will return false for that interfaceId, violating the rule.

For every bytes4 interfaceId equal to type(IERC165).interfaceId the reference contract's supportsInterface(interfaceId) returns true (reports support); the mutant that always returns false will return false for that interfaceId, so the property is that supportsInterface(type(IERC165).interfaceId) must succeed and return true.

For every bytes4 interfaceId input, the reference contract C returns true from supportsInterface exactly when interfaceId equals IERC165 or IAccessControl (i.e., it does not advertise support for arbitrary ids); the mutant violates this by returning true for all ids.

For every bytes4 interfaceId, the reference contract's supportsInterface returns true iff the id equals IERC165 or IAccessControl (i.e., it does not universally return true); the mutant breaks this by returning true for every interfaceId, so there exist ids for which reference returns false but mutant returns true.

For every bytes4 interfaceId, the reference C.supportsInterface(...) returns false for at least some ids (it only advertises IERC165 and IAccessControl), whereas the mutant claims true for every id; thus there exist interfaceId values for which C.supportsInterface(id) == false but the mutant returns true.

For every bytes4 interfaceId, the reference C.supportsInterface(interfaceId) returns either true only for the legitimate supported interfaces (IERC165 or IAccessControl) or false otherwise; the mutant always returns true, so there exist interfaceId values for which C.supportsInterface(interfaceId) == false but the mutant returns true.

For every bytes4 interfaceId, the reference C.supportsInterface(interfaceId) never returns true for arbitrary ids—specifically there exist ids for which the reference returns false but the mutant (which returns true for all ids) returns true; the test fuzzes an interfaceId and asserts that C.supportsInterface(id) is false (a property true for some inputs on the reference but broken by the mutant).

For every interfaceId input, the correct contract returns true iff the id equals IERC165 or IAccessControl (i.e. supportsInterface(type(IERC165).interfaceId) and supportsInterface(type(IAccessControl).interfaceId) are true and other ids false); the mutant inverts the check and thus will return opposite results for some inputs (e.g., IERC165 or IAccessControl), causing the property to fail.

For every bytes4 interfaceId, the reference contract returns true exactly for IERC165 or IAccessControl (i.e. supportsInterface(interfaceId) == (interfaceId == type(IERC165).interfaceId || interfaceId == type(IAccessControl).interfaceId)); the mutant inverts the original check and thus will return different boolean for at least those well-known interface ids.

For every bytes4 interfaceId the reference contract returns true iff interfaceId equals IERC165 or IAccessControl (i.e. supportsInterface(interfaceId) == (interfaceId == type(IERC165).interfaceId || interfaceId == type(IAccessControl).interfaceId)); the mutant negates that check and thus will return a different boolean for those specific interface ids.

For every bytes4 interfaceId, C.supportsInterface(interfaceId) is true exactly when interfaceId equals IERC165 or IAccessControl (i.e. supportsInterface(interfaceId) == (interfaceId == type(IERC165).interfaceId || interfaceId == type(IAccessControl).interfaceId)); the mutant negates that predicate and therefore will disagree for those well-known interface ids.

For every bytes4 interfaceId, C.supportsInterface(interfaceId) returns true exactly when interfaceId equals IERC165 or IAccessControl (i.e. supportsInterface(interfaceId) == (interfaceId == type(IERC165).interfaceId || interfaceId == type(IAccessControl).interfaceId)); the mutant negates that predicate and thus will return the opposite boolean for at least those well-known interface ids.

For any role and account, the correct contract returns true from hasRole iff the internal membership mapping marks the account as a member; the mutant inverts that boolean so there exist inputs (role,account) where hasRole yields the opposite result.
For any role and account, hasRole(role, account) returns the stored membership boolean; the mutant inverts that result, so there exist (role,account) where hasRole differs (true vs false).

For any role and account, the reference contract's hasRole(role, account) returns true exactly when that account is recorded as a member for that role (i.e. C.hasRole mirrors the stored membership); the mutant negates that result so there exist role/account pairs where hasRole returns the opposite boolean.

For any role and account, hasRole(role, account) on the correct contract equals the boolean membership recorded by the contract (so there exists some role/account for which the mutant, which returns the negation, yields the opposite result), and we fuzz role and account to find such a divergence.

For every (role, account) pair, hasRole(role, account) on the correct contract returns the stored membership boolean; the mutant returns the negation, so there exist role/account values for which hasRole differs and the test will detect that by observing a mismatch between two calls that should be identical (idempotent) on the correct contract but flip on the mutant.

For every role and account, the reference contract's hasRole(role, account) returns the stored membership (true iff the account was granted the role via _setupRole in constructor for initial roles, otherwise false); the mutant that always returns true breaks this by returning true for accounts that do not actually have the role.

For any role/address input, the correct contract's hasRole returns whether that account was actually granted the role (via internal storage), whereas the mutant always returns true — so the property is: for any role and account that were NOT granted in the constructor, hasRole(role, account) must be false (the mutant breaks this by returning true for some such account).

For any arbitrary role and account, if that account was not one of the addresses granted PROPOSER_ROLE or EXECUTOR_ROLE in the constructor, then hasRole(role, account) must return false on the correct contract; the mutant (always-true hasRole) will return true for some such inputs.

For any role and account, calling hasRole(role, account) on the correct contract is non-reverting and returns whether the account is recorded as a member (true only for those added in constructor); the mutant that always returns true will make hasRole return true for some accounts that were never granted the role, so there exist fuzzed inputs (role, account) where correct.hasRole(...) != mutant.hasRole(...).

For any role (bytes32) and account (address) that are NOT one of the two addresses granted TIMELOCK_ADMIN_ROLE, PROPOSER_ROLE or EXECUTOR_ROLE in the constructor (i.e. not address(this) and not address(c)), C.hasRole(role, account) always returns false on the reference but the mutant that always returns true will return true for some such fuzzed (role, account).

For any role and account inputs, the reference contract's hasRole correctly returns whether that account is a member (true when role was granted via _setupRole in constructor for given proposers/executors or the timelock admin), whereas the mutant always returns false causing at least one previously-granted role lookup to change from true to false.

For any address A and role R, if the contract's constructor set up A as a member of R (via proposers/executors or timelock admin), then hasRole(R,A) returns true; the mutant always returns false so the property is violated for at least those addresses that were set up as members.

For every role bytes32 r and address a, the reference C returns whether a has role r via hasRole(r,a) (true for accounts that constructor granted); the mutant always returns false, so for some (r,a) where the constructor granted the role the mutant's hasRole differs — test asserts that at least one of the constructor-granted roles is reported true by hasRole for the reference (and thus would fail on the mutant).

For any bytes32 role and address account, the deployed reference C reports membership via hasRole as true for the addresses that the constructor granted (this should return true for at least one known-granted account), whereas the mutant that always returns false will break that rule for those accounts.

For any role R and account A that the constructor granted (TIMELOCK_ADMIN_ROLE was granted to the deployer and the contract itself, and proposers/executors arrays may grant roles), the reference contract's hasRole(R,A) returns true; the mutant that always returns false will violate this by returning false for at least one such (R,A).

For every role and account, hasRole(role, account) in the reference returns whether that exact account is a member (i.e. depends on the supplied account), whereas the mutant always returns membership of address(0) regardless of the supplied account, so there exist inputs (any account ≠ address(0) when address(0)'s membership differs) that produce different return values.
